source_read: Publisher HTML (Wiley Online Library, open access; Drug Alcohol Rev 2023;42(6):1438-1449): structured abstract, key points, Introduction, Methods 2.1-2.6, Results 3.1-3.6, sensitivity analysis, E-values evaluation 5.1-5.2, Tables 1-3 (read as tables), Discussion, Limitations, Conclusion, author contributions, conflict of interest, acknowledgements/funding. Figure 1 (PRISMA) is an image; forest plots (Figure S1) and Tables S1-S4 are in a supporting-information .docx not opened.

claims.overstatement: Mild generalization. The two cohort estimates come from specific populations: a Canadian school cohort followed from grade 10 to grade 11 (Briere 2012) and a US community cohort of HIV-positive and HIV-negative men (Javanbakht 2020), and the outcome is depressive symptoms on CES-D cut-offs, not diagnosed depression. The claim's 'Methamphetamine use is associated with depression' should carry 'depressive symptoms' and the populations.
claims.note: Reproduced from Table 3: Briere 2012 OR 1.60 (1.10-2.30), adjusted for pre-existing individual and contextual factors including depressive symptoms and other substance use; Javanbakht 2020 OR 1.50 (1.10-2.30), adjusted for unemployment, antidepressant use, depressive symptoms at the prior visit and HIV status. Cross-sectional adjusted pool OR 1.66 (1.34-2.05), 4 studies, Q 7.35 (p=0.06, so fixed effect per the paper's rule), I2 59% (Table 2). The claim wisely does not use this review's pooled longitudinal adjusted estimate, which is reported as 1.18 (1.08-1.28) in abstract, Table 2 and Discussion but 1.24 (1.14-1.34) in Results 3.4, and which cannot be obtained from the two adjusted longitudinal estimates in Table 3 (editors' fixed-effect pool of 1.60 and 1.50: 1.55, 1.19-2.01, Q 0.06 vs printed Q 1.76). The general-population (2.0) vs substance-using-sample (1.1) contrast is from McKetin 2019, not this source.

anchors.extracted: Three longitudinal studies: Briere 2012 (Canada, grade 10 to grade 11) OR 1.60 (1.10-2.30), adjusted incl. prior depressive symptoms and other substance use, E-value 2.58 ('low' risk); Javanbakht 2020 (US community cohort, HIV-positive and -negative men, 3.7 years) OR 1.50 (1.10-2.30), adjusted incl. depressive symptoms at prior visit, E-value 2.37 ('low'); Liles 2012 (mothers, 36 months) OR 1.90 (1.00-3.70), unadjusted, E-value 3.21 ('moderate').

Any use, cross-sectional: unadjusted OR 1.40 (1.08-1.80), n 10, I2 77% (random effects); adjusted OR 1.66 (1.34-2.05), n 4, Q 7.35, I2 59% (fixed effect). Nine cross-sectional studies: positive association in 4, none in 5.

anchors.locator: Abstract; Table 2 (longitudinal row); Results 3.4; Discussion, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Pooled longitudinal estimates: unadjusted OR 2.05 (1.53-2.75), n 2; adjusted OR 1.18 (1.08-1.28), n 2, I2 43% (abstract, Table 2, Discussion) but 1.24 (1.14-1.34) in Results 3.4. Neither matches the two adjusted study estimates (1.60 and 1.50).

Only three longitudinal studies, all in sub-populations; premorbid function rarely measured; no dose or frequency analysis possible; no longitudinal data for use disorder; depression could precede use in cross-sectional studies; standard regression adjustment inadequate for strong causal evidence.

key_findings.correction: Editors' reproduction confirmed: fixed effect 1.66 (1.34-2.04), Q 7.40, I2 59%; DerSimonian-Laird 1.85 (1.28-2.69).
Found independently; fixed-effect pool of the two Table 3 adjusted estimates recomputed as 1.55 (1.19-2.01), Q 0.06.
The MSM description of Javanbakht 2020 is supported by that reference's title in the review's reference list.
Count of 11 of 18 low/very-low grades confirmed; Obadeji E-value 2.26 from 1/0.69 vs 2.56 printed confirmed.

reporting_issues.note: Discussion (subpopulation paragraph) cites [7] Colyer among studies 'consistent in reporting significant higher risks'; 3.3 lists it as null; Table 3 OR 1.05 (0.92-1.19).
DiMiceli recent use (4.64, >=50% covariates) should be 'very low' and Mburu CES-D>=23 (3.64, no covariates) 'low' under the printed rules. See missed for two further cases.

Abstract names PubMed, Methods 2.3 Medline; Table 1 labels Casaletto 2015 (people with methamphetamine use disorder from NIDA studies) and Pluddemann 2010 (school students) as general population-based cohorts.
Ref 11 title: 'The influence of familial and non-familial factors on the association between major depression and substance abuse/dependence in 1874 monozygotic male twin pairs'.
Reading limitation; supplement not opened by reader 2 either.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low (several critical items fail, including statistical combination given the irreproducible longitudinal pool).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: E-value reassurance and twin-study causal language outrun the data.

missed: Cross-review inconsistency: Lin 1996's adjusted OR for use disorder and major depression is 2.80 (1.40-5.90) here but 2.8 (0.6-11.8) in McKetin 2019 (Table 2), from an overlapping author group; the interval decides whether the single use-disorder estimate is significant.

Two more E-value grades appear inconsistent with the printed rules: Javanbakht 2020 (adjusted for unemployment, antidepressant use, prior depressive symptoms, HIV status: about 2 of the 5 key covariate groups) and Marshall 2011 (age and injection drug use among the key groups) are graded 'low' with E-values 2.37 and 2.73, which the <50%-covariate rule places in 'moderate' (depends on the unread Table S4).
The review describes Lin 1996 as twin pairs 'in Vietnam'; Table 1 and the reference describe US male twins who served in the military (Vietnam-era registry).

Discussion: 'around 1.5-2 times higher odds ... following methamphetamine use [16-18]' attributed to studies with low confounding risk includes ref 18 (Liles 2012), which is unadjusted and graded 'moderate'.

For cl_meth_depression: the two adjusted cohort ORs (1.60, 1.50) are in adolescents (one-year follow-up, speed/amphetamine exposure) and in a cohort of HIV-positive and HIV-negative MSM; outcome is CES-D-defined depressive symptoms. The claim should carry these populations rather than 'methamphetamine use is associated with depression' generically.
